In the beginning, there were people playing video games.

Then there were websites that reviewed and rated video games.

Those websites hired "journalists" to write supposedly unbiased reviews.

However, those websites were and are supported by advertising from the makers of those games.

So the "journalists" didn't write honest reviews. They wrote reviews that would keep the gaming companies happy, so they wouldn't pull their ads.

Some people started to point this out.

Not much happened.

Then some people pointed out a specific incident that was sort of notable because it wasn't specifically about game companies manipulating "journalism" economically, but was about a specific woman supposedly manipulating the "journalism" through sexual favors.

That, finally, was when it all blew up, since it brought out the real loonies, and more significantly, allowed the gaming sites and the gaming companies and their supporters (both amateur and professional) to pounce on that story and distract attention from the initial charge that the system is fundamentally corrupt. They could, and did, ignore that whole aspect of it and instead focus on the supposed "bigotry" of the people who just wanted honest gaming journalism, because how dare they pick on this poor woman?

Now the whole idea of honest gaming journalism has been pretty much left behind, and the fight, such as it is, is all about feminism and bigotry and social justice and all that swill and nonsense. So the gaming websites can keep right on collecting money from the companies they're supposed to be reviewing without bias, and anyone who tries to say anything about that can immediately be painted as a part of "GamerGate," and therefore a bigot loonie crackpot.
